name: Nora Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work from the box room of a flat I share with my friend Jess, who teaches at a primary school. Mornings are subtitles, Spanish to English, for a company that subcontracts for the streaming platforms, so I'm timing lines on a cooking show or a crime drama. Afternoons I do patient information leaflets and consent forms for a clinical trials agency, which pays better but has a checker who sends back half my sentences. Some days I run a draft through a machine translator first and then fix it, other days I don't bother.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love subtitles when the joke lands in English as well as Spanish, that's a little puzzle I'm proud of. What wears me out is the clock: subtitles pay per programme minute and the rate hasn't moved since I started three years ago. And the medical checker, Rosa, is brilliant but I always feel like a student in front of her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news for anyone who thinks culture needs people, and I'd probably post a clip of a terrible machine subtitle as proof. At the agency I'd be relieved but careful. I wouldn't gloat, because the rates are still bad either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means I keep a job that already doesn't pay enough to save much. The routine stuff it does take over is spotting and timing, which is part of what I'm paid for, so I'd expect the subtitle rate to drop a little more. I'd still be fine for rent, just not getting ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep both clients and try to get a third in medical work, since that's where the money is. I'd do Rosa's terminology course in the spring, which the agency offers for free to freelancers. And I'd keep using the machine draft on the dull leaflets, because it does save me about an hour a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, honestly. Relieved, but it's relief that the bad thing didn't happen, not that anything good did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd not be getting ahead. What would getting ahead look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting ahead would be six months of savings instead of three, and maybe my own flat without a box room office. Jess and I split the rent, which is the only reason I manage. I'd like to stop checking my bank app before I say yes to a drink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you say is responsible for the rate not moving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The platforms, mostly, because they squeeze the subcontractors and the subcontractors squeeze us. I'd like an association that could actually set a minimum rate for subtitles, like they have for some actors. Until then, everyone just takes what's offered.

say: I'd post a **bad machine subtitle** as proof that culture needs people.
I'd be **relieved but careful** at the agency, because rates stay poor.
think: **Spotting and timing** get automated, so I'd expect the subtitle rate to dip.
I'd cover rent but **not get ahead**, with three months saved at most.
do: Look for a **third medical client**, since that work pays more.
Take Rosa's **free terminology course** in the spring.
Keep using the **machine draft** on dull leaflets to save an hour a day.
feel: **Flat relief** that the bad thing didn't happen, not joy.
S0.quote: I'd like to stop checking my bank app before I say yes to a drink.
fieldNote: Her worry is **pay that never rises**, not AI, so calm didn't fit.
Already uses **machine drafts** sometimes, in a practical, unexcited way.
Blames **platforms squeezing subcontractors** and wants a minimum rate.

steps.text: Find a third client for medical leaflets and consent forms
Take the clinical trials agency's free terminology course in spring
Keep running machine drafts on routine leaflets to save an hour daily

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules on this, especially for medicine, because a patient signing a consent form deserves a human check. Online I'd share the subtitlers' association statements and probably argue with tech people in the comments. I'd sound sure of myself, even if I wasn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the subtitle work basically goes. Streaming companies would run the whole thing through software and pay someone like me a tiny amount to glance at it. The medical work might hold because of regulators, but they'd want fewer, more senior checkers like Rosa, not juniors like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the subtitles before they drop me and ask Rosa if the agency trains people as reviewers. I'd learn the post-editing tools properly, maybe a short paid course, around three hundred. I'd join the association and pay the fee, and I'd cut my spending to build up to five months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like I've got time to move, but I'm not sure where the floor is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sound sure online even if you weren't. What's the part you're not sure about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether I'm good enough to be one of the people they keep. I'm three years in and still below the senior people, and a reviewer job needs you to spot what everyone else missed. If the agency only keeps the best twenty percent of translators, I'm not in that group yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first to get to five months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym, which I barely use, and the weekend trips to see my parents by train, which I'd make every other month. I'd also stop buying new books in Spanish and use the library. It sounds small, but that's about a hundred and fifty a month.

say: I'd say **consent forms** need a human check, and push for rules.
I'd share **association statements** and argue with tech people online.
think: The **subtitle work goes**, leaving tiny pay for glancing at software output.
Medical work holds longer but favours **senior reviewers**, not juniors like me.
do: Drop subtitles first and ask Rosa about **reviewer training**.
Take a **post-editing course** for about three hundred.
Cut spending to build up to **five months** of savings.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to move but no clear floor.
S1.quote: If the agency only keeps the best twenty percent of translators, I'm not in that group yet.
fieldNote: Her fear is about **skill rank**: she doubts she's in the top group kept.
Plans to **move before being pushed**, which fits her steady but practical style.
Cuts are specific: **gym, train trips, books**, about a hundred and fifty a month.

steps.text: Ask Rosa about reviewer training at the clinical trials agency
Take a post-editing tools course for about three hundred
Join the subtitlers' association and pay the yearly fee
Cut gym and train trips to reach five months saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments have to slow this down or pay people while it happens, and I'd mean it. I'd go to protests if there were any. At work there'd be no one left to say it to, really, because it'd all be emails from the agency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my career is over by 2028. Subtitles and leaflets are pure thinking work, there's nothing for a robot to wait on. The three years before the robots matter only if I jump to something hands-on now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two years before, I'd look at retraining as a speech and language therapy assistant, because it uses languages and you work with people face to face. I'd save hard, maybe move back near my parents to cut rent. After it arrives, I'd take whatever support exists and join whatever group is organising for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, mostly. I feel a bit stupid for choosing languages when everyone was telling me to do computing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said moving back near your parents. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would be thrilled and my dad would ask if I'm giving up. They live in a small town two hours away, where rent is half what I pay. Jess would have to find a new flatmate, which I'd feel bad about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the robot timing that helps you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I pick a job where hands matter. A therapy assistant does a lot of talking, which is thinking work, so maybe I'd only get those three years if I did something more physical, like care. I honestly don't know enough to pick right.

say: I'd say governments must **slow it** or pay people while it happens.
I'd join **protests** if any were organised.
think: My career is **over by 2028**, since it's all thinking work.
The robots' **three-year gap** only helps if I jump to hands-on work now.
do: Look into retraining as a **speech therapy assistant**.
Move back near her parents to **halve her rent**.
Lean on **support schemes** and join groups pushing for basic income.
feel: **Scared**, and a bit foolish for choosing languages over computing.
S2.quote: I feel a bit stupid for choosing languages when everyone was telling me to do computing.
fieldNote: She grasps that her work is **all thinking work** with no robot buffer.
Unsure which **hands-on route** would actually last; she says so honestly.
Moving home is a real **money move**, not just comfort.

steps.text: Look into training as a speech and language therapy assistant
Move back to her parents' town, where rent is half
Apply for whatever income support the government sets up
Join a group campaigning for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, and the platforms and agencies should help fund retraining for the people whose work they use. I'd say that at association meetings. I'd say it to my MP too, in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think it gives me time to be clever about it. I'd keep earning from translation for two or three years while it still pays, and spend the time building the next thing. But I'm a steady person, I'd want to see what others do first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the therapy assistant course part-time in year two, once I'd seen whether people were actually getting hired from it. I'd keep the medical client as long as possible because it's the steadiest money. I'd write to my MP about a retraining fund and push the association to do the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit sad, but I'd have a list, and lists help me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see what others do. Who would you be watching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Sofía from university went into in-house localisation at a bank, and she'd know first if things were turning. And if the agency starts letting Rosa, our senior medical checker, go, then I'll know it's real. I'd move the moment one of them moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the flat with Jess in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay, because the rent split is what lets me save. Maybe in year four I'd move home if the money ran thin. Jess and I joke about it, but she's worried about teaching too.

say: I'd say **platforms and agencies** should fund retraining for translators.
I'd write to **my MP** and say it at association meetings.
think: Five years lets me **earn and plan** at the same time.
Being steady, I'd **watch others** before I jump.

Keep the **medical client** as long as it lasts.
Write to her MP about a **retraining fund**.
feel: **Uneasy and sad**, but steadied by having a list.
S3.quote: If the agency starts letting Rosa, our senior medical checker, go, then I'll know it's real.
fieldNote: She uses **friends as signals**: Sofía at the bank and Rosa at the agency.
Five years gives her a **staged plan**, which lowers her from alarmed to anxious.

steps.text: Start a part-time therapy assistant course in year two
Keep the clinical trials client as long as work comes
Write to her MP asking for a retraining fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for a fair transition, and if it isn't fair, that's a choice someone made. I'd want the association planning for it now, with the universities. I'd be a bit less angry online, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I could build a proper second career and still be in my thirties. I'd translate until maybe 2030, then switch. The worry is that everyone else would have the same idea, so the retraining places fill up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the full speech therapy degree part-time from 2028, not just the assistant course. I'd keep one translation client and stop subtitles once the rate falls below what makes sense. I'd keep saving, maybe fifty a month extra, and stay in the flat with Jess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly, and a bit hopeful. It's a long runway, and I'd have time to change my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the retraining places might fill up. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Apply early, before it's obvious, which goes against how I usually do things. I'd probably need someone to push me. Jess would push me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to be a translator in that world, if you could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In a way, yes. I like words, but I'd rather do something people need from a person. Wanting it isn't the same as being paid for it.

I'd want the association and **universities planning** now.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to pick the right new job and I'd probably pick wrong. What would help is a paid retraining place with a wage, and someone telling me honestly which jobs will still need people. I don't need cheering up, I need good information.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'd still be a translator if pay were fair. I think I'd stay in a heartbeat if subtitles paid properly. Part of this is AI and part of it is that translation work was already badly paid.

headlineQuote: Part of this is AI and part of it is that translation work was already badly paid.
portrait: A **27-year-old** Spanish–English subtitler and medical translator sharing a flat with her friend Jess.
Uses **machine drafts** now and then, and watches friends before making any move.
Worried about **flat rates** even when AI stalls, and about not being in the top group kept.
In the AGI pictures she plans a move into **speech therapy**, longer and better with more time.
Blames **platforms and agencies** more than the technology itself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to pick the right new job.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid retraining place** with a wage while studying.
**Honest information** on which jobs will still need people.
